channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: Track the next US CPI print after the oil spike, whether the dropped Hormuz toll stays dead while the Iran blockade holds, the India-EU FTA legal review, the scale of VW’s restructuring, and the AfD-watched Saxony-Anhalt state election.
item.description:
• US CPI release (mid-July): June came in at 3.5%, but the post-survey oil spike means the next print is the real test of whether energy is reigniting inflation and forcing a July or September Fed hike.
  • Hormuz — does the toll stay dead? Trump dropped the 20% fee for promised Gulf investment, but the blockade on Iran persists; watch whether the fee idea returns and whether the promised Gulf investments are new money.
  • India-EU FTA legal review: India says it could be the bloc's fastest-ever deal; a conclusion would extend the bilateral bloc-building trend and redirect trade flows toward Europe.
  • VW restructuring scale: Blume's ~50,000-job figure is a first estimate; the confirmed plan will show how far the shock spreads through Europe's auto supply chain.
  • Saxony-Anhalt state election: the feared AfD advance — and the dispute over its access to security information — is a near-term marker for Germany's political direction alongside Le Pen's 2027 momentum in France.

item.title: CENTCOM confirmed three Corsair unmanned surface vessels struck Iran's Bandar Abbas naval base — the first combat use of US sea drones — with analysts linking the shift to depleted US missile stocks and autonomous tactics proven in Ukraine.
item.description:
The tactical debut has strategic weight. The robotic surface vessels can be remotely piloted or navigate autonomously using AI, radar and onboard sensors, and their use signals that unmanned, software-defined systems are moving from the periphery to the front line of naval operations. Argentine and Pakistani analysts tie the move to a worrying reduction in the Pentagon's missile inventory, making low-cost autonomous platforms a resource-efficient alternative. It is the clearest sign yet that the Iran conflict is also a proving ground for the next generation of AI-enabled military hardware.

Industry Impact

The relevance for ACS is the accelerating shift toward unmanned and autonomous defence platforms, a fast-growing niche for lightweight structural adhesives, protective coatings and sealants engineered for drones and USVs rather than crewed vessels. It reinforces the broader defence-demand tailwind (see other insight in this alert) and points to specialised, high-value material requirements — corrosion, marine and electronics-protection chemistries — as autonomous systems scale.

The Economic Times | Middle East Monitor | Pakistan Observer | La Nacion

item.title: Pakistan imposed five-year anti-dumping duties on soda ash from Turkey and Kenya, Ahlstrom launched a high-density release paper for self-adhesive labels, and Germany's VCI opened a nationwide circular-economy roadshow.
item.description:
Each is a direct-industry data point rather than a macro read. Pakistan's National Tariff Commission set duties of 13.54% (Kenya) and 4.49-6.58% (Turkey) on disodium carbonate, a basic feedstock for glass, detergents and chemicals — another example of trade barriers reaching upstream chemical inputs. Ahlstrom's MaxLiner targets the self-adhesive labelling chain with a renewable-fibre release paper suited to silicone coating and lamination. And the VCI's Chemie³ "Circular Economy Roadshow," themed "opportunity in challenging times," signals the German industry positioning circularity as competitive advantage amid weak demand. Taiwanese chemical-fibre plants running near full capacity on semiconductor-materials demand round out a mixed but active picture.

Industry Impact

These are the most directly relevant items of the day for an adhesives, coatings and sealants producer. Soda-ash duties reshape regional feedstock sourcing economics; Ahlstrom's launch is a competitive move in the self-adhesive segment worth benchmarking; and the VCI circular-economy drive previews the recyclability and mono-material design requirements increasingly shaping adhesive and coating chemistries in Europe. Track the circular-economy agenda as a product-development driver, not only a compliance cost.

Business Recorder | Bumprom.ru | VCI | Commercial Times

item.title: Seoul raised its 2026 GDP forecast to 3% — its strongest in five years, up from 2% — on surging AI-chip demand for Samsung and SK Hynix, projecting a record USD 290bn current-account surplus, though it nudged inflation up to 2.6% on higher oil.
item.description:
The upgrade is a rare bright spot against a slowing developed-market picture, and it is narrowly sourced: the semiconductor cycle is doing the work, with a supplementary budget cushioning war-driven energy costs. The AI supply-chain strength extends beyond chips — in Taiwan, Citi tracks broad-based June gains across test interfaces (+94%), copper-clad laminates and PCBs (+55%) and cooling (+65%), and Korea's Samsung/SK Hynix are anchoring an 800-trillion-won chip hub. The vulnerability is concentration: growth this dependent on one capex cycle is exposed if AI investment cools.

Industry Impact

The electronics AI build-out is one of the few expanding demand pools for high-value ACS — semiconductor-grade materials, electronics adhesives, thermal-interface and encapsulation chemistries, and materials for advanced packaging and liquid cooling. Korea and Taiwan are the key geographies. The risk mirrors the reward: exposure concentrated in a single AI-capex cycle, so treat electronics-linked ACS demand as high-growth but cyclically fragile.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt | Financial Post | Daily Sabah

item.title: Ten countries including Germany, France and the UK launched a joint anti-ballistic-missile alliance at the Paris summit, while Germany's air force chief insisted Europe still needs US weapons and Pistorius flagged EUR 35bn for military space.
item.description:
The build-up and its fault lines appear together. The new alliance aims to fill gaps in European missile defence through shared industrial and technical cooperation, and Germany's EUR 35bn space-defence commitment signals scale. But the German air force chief warned Europe cannot yet replace proven US systems — a direct tension with EU rules capping non-EU (including US) participation in jointly financed projects at 35%. Meanwhile allied agencies warned that Russian FSB-linked hackers continue targeting critical infrastructure across energy, defence and communications, keeping the threat live.

Industry Impact

Defence is a rising demand pillar for specialty ACS — structural adhesives, protective and stealth coatings, and sealants for missiles, aircraft, drones and space hardware. Accelerating European procurement is a multi-year tailwind, but the US-versus-EU sourcing split means multiple national supply chains rather than one scale programme, favouring suppliers able to serve several national primes. The infrastructure-sabotage warnings reinforce the case for OT-security and energy-resilience investment at chemical sites.

Beijing Daily | Politico Europe | MarketScreener | Herald Sun

item.title: An IMF study finds many European states on an unsustainable path: the debt burden of an average European country could double within 15 years if tax and spending policies stay unchanged, driven by defence, demographics and the green transition.
item.description:
The pressure points are structural and simultaneous. NATO's newly agreed 3.5%-of-GDP defence target adds spending just as ageing populations lift health and pension costs and the green transformation demands public investment. The IMF's prescription — grow via reform while cutting deficits — is the hard combination most European governments have struggled to deliver. It sharpens the fiscal backdrop to Europe's rearmament (see other insight in this alert) and its industrial-policy ambitions, both of which assume fiscal space that this study questions.

Industry Impact

Constrained European public finances shape ACS demand through the channels that depend on state spending: infrastructure, public construction and subsidised green-transition projects. Tighter budgets cap the upside from stimulus-driven construction-chemicals demand and raise the risk that industrial-support programmes are trimmed. The strategic read for a European-headquartered producer is to avoid over-indexing to demand that relies on sustained public expenditure Europe may not be able to afford.

Suddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: The India-UK CETA enters into force 15 July with duty-free access for nearly 99% of Indian exports, India says an EU FTA could be the fastest in the bloc's history, and New Delhi and London are negotiating the UK's 2027 carbon border tax.
item.description:
This converts a watch item from the prior run into a live event. CETA cuts duties on 90% of UK goods and 99% of Indian exports, benefiting UK vehicles and spirits and Indian textiles, leather and auto components, plus a social-security pact for 75,000+ Indian professionals. India frames it as a template for Western deals: an India-EU FTA is in final legal review and could redirect USD 10-11bn of Indian exports from the US to Europe, while CBAM talks address a mechanism that could tax 14-24% of the value of steel, aluminium and cement exports. The pattern is bilateral bloc-building as the multilateral order fragments.

Industry Impact

The signal for ACS producers is a re-mapping of tariff geography: supply chains routed through India, the UK and the EU gain preferential access, and India strengthens as a manufacturing-footprint and demand-growth destination as global firms diversify sourcing. The looming UK and EU carbon border taxes are the caveat — they raise the landed cost of carbon-intensive inputs, so sourcing footprints and feedstock choices should be re-evaluated for both tariff and carbon exposure.

The Times of India | South China Morning Post | The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times

item.title: China's January-June foreign trade rose 16.9% to CNY 25.47tn, with imports up 22.1%, mechanical and electrical exports up 20.1% and computing-power hardware trade up 56.6% — and Beijing signalled it will actively expand imports under its 2026-30 plan.
item.description:
The composition matters more than the headline. Growth is concentrated in high-tech, exportable manufacturing: computing hardware, electronics and AI-powered robotics (China's exports have risen over 10% for an 11th straight quarter, with bionic robots now shipping to 90+ countries). EU-China trade grew 10.2% in H1, and Beijing's pledge to boost imports during the 15th Five-Year Plan is aimed partly at easing trade tensions. This is the mechanism behind the Western decoupling debate (see other insight in this alert): China is deepening, not loosening, its grip on advanced-manufacturing supply.

Industry Impact

A stronger Chinese export machine is double-edged for ACS producers. The electronics, EV and robotics surge lifts demand for high-value electronics and automotive adhesives — but increasingly served by Chinese domestic suppliers moving up the value chain, including into the specialty inputs Western firms sell. Beijing's import-expansion signal may open near-term opportunities; the longer-term threat is intensifying Chinese competition in exactly the high-margin ACS segments that matter most.

China Daily | The Economic Times | MarketScreener | Global Times

item.title: EU tariffs are reshoring Western EV output (Chinese-built share down from 38% to 23%), yet Italy's industry minister warned the Volkswagen crisis — with potential cuts of around 50,000 jobs — risks overwhelming Europe's entire automotive supply chain.
item.description:
The two forces pull in opposite directions. EU punitive duties of 7.8-35.3% pushed BMW, Volvo, Smart, Tesla and Dacia to shift output back to Europe, while Chinese brands pivoted to untaxed plug-in hybrids (BYD and GAC lifting their EU PHEV share to 13% from 3%). That is constructive for European assembly. But VW CEO Oliver Blume's first quantification of the cuts — around 50,000 jobs absent lower labour costs — prompted minister Urso to warn the damage spans all major European carmakers and their suppliers. Meanwhile China's monthly car exports topped 1m for the first time (see other insight in this alert), keeping pricing pressure on.

Industry Impact

Automotive is a core ACS end-market, and the signal is mixed. Reshored EV and component production is a direct positive for European automotive adhesives, coatings and sealants, but a supply-chain-wide contraction at VW and its peers would remove volume faster than reshoring adds it. Position for reshoring-linked demand while stress-testing exposure to the German and Italian OEM base most at risk of restructuring.

Frankfurter Rundschau | ANSA | The Guardian | The Hindu Business Line

item.title: An EY-Parthenon study estimates the West would need USD 23.6tn over 25 years to cut reliance on China — the US USD 13.7tn, the Eurozone USD 9.1tn (twice its annual budget) and the UK USD 800bn — even as polls show support tilting to China.
item.description:
The figure quantifies what "de-risking" actually costs: rebuilding manufacturing, restoring research capacity and constructing alternative supply networks by 2050. It lands alongside a Business Standard argument that Chinese mercantilism has been "the mother of all shocks" to the global economy, and GlobeScan/Gallup polling showing China's standing as preferred leading power rising to 33-36% while US approval falls to a record-low reading. The through-line: decoupling is a generational, capital-intensive project, not a near-term switch, and the West's leverage is eroding while the bill grows.

Industry Impact

Supply-chain reconfiguration on this scale is the defining structural backdrop for ACS producers. It implies decades of relocation-driven demand for construction and manufacturing inputs in the West and allied economies, but also sustained input-cost inflation as lower-cost Chinese supply is designed out. The strategic read: position for a slow, expensive reshoring cycle — real incremental demand where new capacity is built, offset by higher feedstock and intermediate costs across the transition.

Beijing Daily | Business Standard | Chinatimes

item.title: The US refunded USD 81bn in tariffs this fiscal year after the Supreme Court ruled them illegal — pushing the June deficit to USD 120bn — while a separate report finds USD 83bn of clean-energy and manufacturing investment cancelled or delayed.
item.description:
Two reversals point the same way. The tariff refunds (up from USD 5bn a year earlier, concentrated in May-June) widened the nine-month federal gap 2% to USD 1.37tn and inject fresh uncertainty into US trade policy, since duties already collected are being clawed back. In parallel, BlueGreen Alliance counts 223 stalled or cancelled clean-energy and manufacturing projects (111,765 jobs) after Biden-era incentives were repealed, with 3,034 more projects facing tighter tax-credit rules. Together they show US industrial-investment conditions loosening on tariffs but tightening on green manufacturing.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers the tariff refunds signal that the US tariff regime is legally contestable and less predictable — a planning risk for anyone pricing long-term US supply on current duty assumptions. The clean-energy pullback is more direct: cancelled battery, EV and renewables projects shrink a fast-growing demand pool for structural adhesives, coatings and sealants in the US. Weight US growth assumptions toward established end-markets rather than the green-manufacturing build-out now losing federal support.

The Independent | The Straits Times | MarketScreener | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: US inflation slowed to 3.5% in June on lower petrol prices during the brief ceasefire, but the renewed Hormuz oil spike has pushed pump prices back up — lifting the odds of a July Fed hike to 46.5%, with about 60% priced for September.
item.description:
June's print reflected a moment that has passed: the gasoline relief behind it came from the ceasefire, which has since collapsed, and the national average has ticked back to USD 3.87/gallon. TD Securities now sees the risk skewed toward hikes rather than cuts into late 2026. This is the domestic mirror of the global fossilflation read (see other insight in this alert): cooling core data undercut by an energy shock that arrived after the survey window.

Industry Impact

A Fed leaning toward holding or hiking pressures the rate-sensitive end-markets ACS depends on — US housing and autos. Combined with oil-driven feedstock inflation, that is margin-negative on both sides of the P&L. US-exposed coatings and adhesives demand should be planned cautiously for H2, and any renewed Hormuz escalation would reinforce the hawkish path and deepen the demand drag.

The Straits Times | BNN Bloomberg | The Economic Times | Cnyes

item.title: Brent leapt 9.6% to USD 83.30 on the blockade, and forecasters responded: Atradius cut 2026 global growth to 2.4%, Esade sees energy prices up to 80% higher and inflation at 4.4%, and the OECD warned of rising inflation and weaker growth.
item.description:
The move reverses the "markets shrugged it off" reading of recent runs. The single-day Brent jump was its largest on record, and the pass-through is now the story: the OECD and Al Jazeera frame it as "fossilflation" — the repeated inflationary hit to economies still tied to imported fossil fuels. Crucially, Atradius's benign 2.4% baseline assumes a gradual Hormuz reopening, exactly the assumption the day's blockade undercuts, so the downside skew is real. The toll's withdrawal (see other insight in this alert) may cap the freight-cost channel, but crude has already repriced.

Industry Impact

Higher oil is the core transmission into ACS economics: crude and naphtha set feedstock costs for adhesives, coatings and sealants, and rising energy prices lift drying, curing and logistics bills across every plant. A downgraded global growth path compounds the squeeze by softening end-market demand in construction and manufacturing. Plan H2 conservatively for both margin (input inflation) and volume (weaker demand), and hedge energy exposure where contract structures allow.

Le Figaro | Financial Post | El Pais | Al Jazeera

item.title: The US declared it would take over the Strait of Hormuz with a reimposed Iran blockade and a 20% cargo toll — then, a day later, Trump withdrew the toll for promised Gulf investment deals, narrowing the blockade to Iranian ships only.
item.description:
The delta since the last alert is a fee that came and went inside 24 hours. On 13 July Trump announced a full naval blockade and a 20% charge on all Hormuz cargo, framed as reimbursement for US security; CENTCOM said enforcement would begin immediately. By 14 July the toll was gone — replaced by promised Gulf-state investment into US factories — while a full blockade remains on ships to or from Iranian ports. The reversal followed sharp pushback: the German Shipowners' Association called the fee legally impermissible, and shipping bodies warned it would deter transit. The net position is calmer than the headline: the strait stays open to non-Iranian traffic without a toll, but the blockade and the underlying conflict persist.

Industry Impact

For the chemical and ACS industry the transmission runs through energy and freight, not direct exposure. The toll's withdrawal removes a would-be de-facto tariff on every Hormuz-routed input, but the oil-price spike it triggered (see other insight in this alert) still lifts feedstock, naphtha and shipping-insurance costs. Procurement should treat the fee as a live policy risk that can reappear, and continue to stress-test Gulf-routed petrochemical and base-oil supply against a blockade that has not been lifted.

POLITICO | The Times of India | Handelsblatt | Wirtschafts Woche | The Boston Globe

item.title: MIA Digest: The US declared a Hormuz blockade and 20% cargo toll, then dropped the toll within a day for Gulf investment deals; oil jumped over 9%, forecasters cut global growth, and the US refunded USD 81bn of court-struck tariffs.
item.description:
• Hormuz toll reversed: the US declared a blockade and a 20% cargo toll, then Trump dropped the toll within a day for promised Gulf investment, keeping a full blockade only on Iran.
  • Oil shock, darker macro: Brent jumped 9.6% to USD 83; Atradius cut 2026 global growth to 2.4% and the OECD warned of energy-driven “fossilflation.”
  • US tariffs unwind: Washington refunded USD 81bn after the Supreme Court ruled the tariffs illegal, widening the June federal deficit to USD 120bn.
  • Decoupling’s price tag: an EY-Parthenon study puts the cost of cutting Western dependence on China at USD 23.6tn over 25 years.
  • India trade goes live: the India-UK CETA takes effect 15 July with duty-free access for 99% of Indian exports, as an India-EU FTA nears conclusion.
